newsitem.title: USA: Rocky Mountain snowstorm halts search for pilot.
newsitem.headline: Rocky Mountain snowstorm halts search for pilot.

text.p: A blinding, wind-driven snowstorm Thursday forced rescuers to halt their search for the pilot of an A-10 warplane that was found on a Rocky Mountain peak more than two weeks after it disappeared.

Air Force spokeswoman Lt. Col. Robin Chandler said the search for Capt. Craig Button, 32, had been abandoned only temporarily. "We are determining right now whether the two para-rescue teams can undertake another mission later today."
Blinding snow conditions had abated by early afternoon, she said, but the mountain tops were still shrouded in clouds.

The aircraft disappeared during a routine training mission April 2 and Air Force officials have been at a loss to explain why the pilot left the three-plane delta formation in which he was flying and apparently veered northeast into Colorado, some 850 miles away from a training exercise.

Chandler said the two para-rescue teams, each made up of two men, were dropped by an MH-53 heavy-lift helicopter in a natural bowl 1,000 feet below the wreckage Wednesday and had intended to climb up to the plane after spending the night on the mountain.
"They never made it to the plane," she said. Instead, the MH-53 braved the storm to pick the four men up and bring them back to the A-10 search headquarters in Eagle, Colorado.

Earlier, Air Force Maj. Gen. Nels Running told reporters he did not know when the search would resume but stressed it would continue until Button was found. "We don't close the books until we have conclusion," he said.
Nels also indicated it was possible Button's body might not be found with his plane.

"The search for the pilot will continue until the disposition of the pilot is known," he said. "Evidence that he is not within the aircraft may be a little bit more difficult to obtain ... But the search will continue. Where? When? How? I can't tell you all of those things."

The wreckage was spotted Sunday by an Army National Guard helicopter crew near a steep cliff on New York Mountain in the remote Sawatch range southeast of the Vail ski resort. The Air Force confirmed Wednesday that it was indeed the missing A-10.

Button, whose plane was carrying four 500-pound (225-kg) Mark 82 conventional bombs, broke formation after leaving the Davis-Monthan Air Force Base near Tucson, Arizona, headed for the Barry M. Goldwater Bombing Range in Arizona.
